title: The Wampanoag-Plymouth alliance
description: An epidemic of 1616 to 1619 emptied Patuxet, where Plymouth was built in 1620; Ousamequin (Massasoit) allied with Plymouth in 1621 against the Narragansett, and Tisquantum interpreted.

facts.text: Between 1616 and 1619 an epidemic ravaged the Wampanoag and neighboring peoples, emptying Tisquantum's home village of Patuxet.
The Mayflower colonists founded Plymouth in 1620 on the site of Patuxet.
The epidemic left the Wampanoag vulnerable to the Narragansett, who had escaped it; English guns and soldiers could help against them.
In 1621 the Wampanoag leader Ousamequin, called Massasoit by the English, and Plymouth agreed to defend each other and to trade.
Tisquantum (Squanto) of Patuxet was kidnapped by an English captain to be sold as a slave in Spain, escaped to England and learned English.
Tisquantum came home in 1619 to find his people wiped out by disease, and later served Plymouth as its interpreter.

title: The 1621 harvest and the Thanksgiving story
description: In fall 1621 about 90 Wampanoag men and about 50 colonists shared a harvest celebration over several days; the national Thanksgiving holiday dates from 1863, and since 1970 some Native people mark a National Day of Mourning.

facts.text: In fall 1621 about 90 Wampanoag men led by Ousamequin joined about 50 colonists at Plymouth's harvest celebration for several days, bringing venison.
The 1621 gathering is commonly called the first Thanksgiving, but Lincoln proclaimed Thanksgiving a national holiday only in 1863.
Since 1970 Native people and supporters have gathered at Plymouth on Thanksgiving Day for a National Day of Mourning.

title: A city upon a hill
description: In 1630 John Winthrop led Puritans to found the Massachusetts Bay Colony, a model community with a purified church that he said would be watched as a city upon a hill.

facts.text: In 1630 John Winthrop, governor of the Massachusetts Bay Colony, led a fleet of mostly Puritan settlers to New England.
The Puritans wanted a godly society and a church purified of what they saw as corruptions in the Church of England.
In his 1630 sermon A Model of Christian Charity, Winthrop said the colony would be "a city upon a hill", with all the world watching it.

title: Banished dissenters
description: Massachusetts banished Roger Williams in 1635 for his views on conscience and Native land; he founded Providence. Anne Hutchinson, convicted in 1637, went to Aquidneck in 1638.

facts.text: Roger Williams argued that magistrates had no right to rule consciences, and that Native people, not the king's charter, truly owned the land.
Massachusetts banished Williams in 1635; the Narragansett sold him land, and he founded Providence, open to people of all faiths.
Anne Hutchinson held weekly meetings of Boston women to discuss sermons and share her own religious views.
Convicted in 1637 of slandering the colony's ministers, Hutchinson was banished and in 1638 helped found a settlement on Aquidneck, now in Rhode Island.

title: Three colonial regions
description: New England lived by small farms, fishing, shipbuilding and trade; the Middle Colonies were the grain-growing breadbasket; the Southern Colonies grew tobacco, rice and indigo with enslaved labor.

facts.text: New England's rocky soil and cold winters suited small family farms, so colonists turned to fishing, lumbering, shipbuilding and trade.
The Middle Colonies were called the breadbasket colonies: their fertile soil grew enough wheat and other grain to export.
The Middle Colonies drew an unusually diverse mix of settlers, including Germans and Scots-Irish as well as English.
In the Chesapeake colonies of Virginia and Maryland planters grew tobacco; in the Carolinas and Georgia, rice and indigo.
Southern plantations came to rely on the forced labor of enslaved Africans.

title: Pennsylvania's holy experiment
description: In 1681 Charles II granted the Quaker William Penn a charter for Pennsylvania, which Penn opened to people of all faiths.

facts.text: In 1681 Charles II granted the Quaker William Penn a charter for Pennsylvania, which Penn opened to people of all faiths.

title: The first Africans in English Virginia
description: In 1619 the White Lion brought 20 and odd Africans to Point Comfort, Virginia; their legal status was unclear, and some, like Anthony Johnson, became free landowners.

facts.text: In late August 1619 the English ship White Lion brought "20 and odd" Africans to Point Comfort, Virginia.
The legal status of these first Africans in Virginia is unclear: they may have been enslaved for life or freed after years of service.
Anthony Johnson, listed as "Antonio the Negro" in 1625, gained his freedom and became a landowner among free Africans in Northampton County.

title: Slavery written into law
description: Colonial courts and laws made slavery race-based and lifelong (John Punch), legal (Massachusetts, 1641) and inherited through the mother (Virginia, 1662).

facts.text: After three servants ran away in Virginia, a court gave the two white men extra years, but sentenced John Punch, an African, to serve for life.
In 1641 Massachusetts became the first English colony to legalize slavery, in its Body of Liberties.
A 1662 Virginia law made a child enslaved or free according to the mother's status, reversing the English rule that status followed the father.

title: The scale of the Middle Passage
description: SlaveVoyages estimates about 12.5 million Africans were forced aboard ships and about 10.7 million survived; about 388,000 landed directly in mainland North America.

facts.text: SlaveVoyages database estimates: about 12.5 million Africans were forced aboard ships to the Americas, and about 10.7 million survived the crossing.
The gap between those two estimates means roughly 1.8 million people died during the Middle Passage.
About 388,000 survivors were landed directly in mainland North America, a small share; most were landed in the Caribbean and South America.

title: Enduring and resisting the Middle Passage
description: Olaudah Equiano's 1789 narrative describes captives chained below deck amid filth and death; captives revolted on about one ship in ten.

facts.text: Olaudah Equiano, once enslaved and later free, wrote in his 1789 autobiography of captives kept below deck in chains and filth, amid "the shrieks of the women, and the groans of the dying".
Captives rose in revolt on about one slave ship in ten, most often while the ship was still near the African coast; few revolts succeeded.

title: Why Metacom went to war
description: Metacom, Massasoit's son, recorded grievances over lost land, English cattle and unequal courts; Plymouth's execution of three Wampanoag men in 1675 set off the war.

facts.text: Metacom, whom the English called King Philip, was a Wampanoag sachem and a son of Massasoit, who had greeted Plymouth's colonists in 1621.
In June 1675 Metacom told John Easton of Rhode Island his people's complaints: lost land, English cattle ruining their crops, unfair English courts.
The war began after Plymouth hanged three Wampanoag men in June 1675 for the murder of John Sassamon, a Christian convert and interpreter.
The Wampanoag, Nipmuc and Narragansett fought the colonists, while the Mohegan and Pequot fought alongside the English.

title: What King Philip's War cost
description: Metacom was killed in August 1676; about 600 English soldiers died and 17 settlements were destroyed, while thousands of Native people died and many were sold into slavery.

facts.text: Colonial forces under Benjamin Church killed Metacom in August 1676.
About 600 English colonists were killed and many towns destroyed; thousands of Native people were killed, and many were sold into slavery.
For the size of the population, King Philip's War was one of the bloodiest wars in American history.

title: Coverture and women's work
description: Under coverture a married woman's legal identity merged into her husband's; unmarried women and widows (femes soles) could own property and run businesses; households ran on women's work.

facts.text: Under coverture, from English law, a married woman's legal existence merged into her husband's: she could not make contracts or sue in her own name.
Unmarried women and widows, called femes soles, could own property, make contracts and run businesses in their own names.
Colonial households ran on women's work: cooking, cleaning, spinning, weaving, sewing, and making butter and soap.

title: Eliza Lucas Pinckney and indigo
description: At 16 Eliza Lucas managed her father's South Carolina plantations and developed indigo, which became the colony's second most lucrative crop, grown and processed by enslaved people.

facts.text: Around 1739 Eliza Lucas, 16, was left to manage her father's Wappoo Plantation near Charleston and two larger South Carolina estates.
After trying crops such as ginger and cotton, she grew a successful indigo crop, and indigo became South Carolina's second most lucrative crop after rice.
In colonial South Carolina, enslaved people did almost all the work of growing indigo and turning it into dye, skilled work learned through long experience.

title: Colonial assemblies and town meetings
description: Virginia's House of Burgesses (1619), the Mayflower Compact (1620) and New England town meetings gave colonists elected self-government, though voting was limited to property-owning white men.

facts.text: Virginia's House of Burgesses first met at Jamestown on July 30, 1619, the first elected assembly in English America.
Before landing in 1620, 41 men aboard the Mayflower signed the Mayflower Compact, forming a "civil body politic" to make laws.
In New England town meetings, a town's voters gathered to elect local officials and vote on taxes and spending.
Colonial voters were usually white men who owned property; women, enslaved people and Native people were shut out.

title: Salutary neglect and the power of the purse
description: Britain loosely enforced its rules (Burke's 'salutary neglect'), and colonial assemblies controlled taxes and governors' salaries.

facts.text: Colonial assemblies controlled taxes and spending, including the royal governor's salary, which they could withhold.
In 1775 Edmund Burke credited the colonies' success to Britain's "wise and salutary neglect": its loose enforcement of rules.

title: The French and Indian War
description: From 1754 to 1763 Britain and France, each with Native allies, fought for eastern North America as part of the Seven Years' War; Franklin's Albany Plan failed; Britain won Canada and the land east of the Mississippi.

facts.text: In 1754 George Washington led Virginia troops to drive the French from the Ohio Valley; outnumbered, he surrendered at Fort Necessity.
The French and Indian War (1754 to 1763) was the North American part of a wider war between Britain and France, the Seven Years' War.
France fought with many Native allies, such as the Shawnee, while Britain's main Native partner was the Iroquois Confederacy.
At Albany in 1754, Benjamin Franklin proposed uniting the colonies under one council; the colonial assemblies and the Crown rejected it.
In the 1763 Treaty of Paris, Britain gained Canada and all French lands east of the Mississippi, and Florida from Spain.

title: Victory and debt
description: The war nearly doubled Britain's debt, and Britain wanted the colonies to help pay; Pontiac's War of 1763 led Britain to bar settlement west of the Appalachians.

facts.text: The war nearly doubled Britain's national debt, and Britain expected the colonies to help pay it off.
In 1763 Native nations of the Great Lakes and Ohio Valley attacked British forts in Pontiac's War; Britain then barred colonists from settling farther west.

title: Freedom and slavery from the same year
description: In 1619 Virginia gained both the first elected assembly in English America and its first recorded Africans: self-government and slavery grew up together in the colonies.

facts.text: Virginia's first elected assembly and its first recorded Africans both arrived in 1619, a year before Plymouth was founded.
